item.title: Marin County to test AlertMarin emergency alerts at 10 a.m. Sept. 26; fewer than half of Tiburon, Belvedere households signed up
item.description: Marin County will test AlertMarin, its emergency notification system, at 10 a.m. Sept. 26, sending a test alert to everyone registered for the service.
item.content:encoded:
Marin County will test AlertMarin, its emergency notification system, at 10 a.m. Sept. 26, sending a test alert to everyone registered for the service.

The test checks that AlertMarin can get critical information out in an emergency, according to the county Office of Emergency Management, part of the Marin County Fire Department. Belvedere, in a notice urging residents to sign up, also cited the approach of peak wildfire season and the El Niño forecast.

Subscribers will get the test by whatever contact methods they chose — text message, phone call or email — in English or Spanish, depending on their account settings. Anyone who doesn’t receive it should log in atalertmarin.organd check that their contact information and addresses are current, the county said.

Fewer than half of Tiburon and Belvedere households will get it. In Tiburon, 1,782 households, or 48%, have a subscription, and in Belvedere 456, or 45.5%, according to the office’s AlertMarin subscriber dashboard.

The rate falls by more than half in multiunit properties, where just 110 of Tiburon’s 588 housing units, or 18.7%, and 29 of Belvedere’s 136, or 21.3%, have at least one household subscriber. Tiburon has 2,716 individual subscribers in all and Belvedere 675.

AlertMarin sends real-time instructions during wildfires, floods, evacuations and other emergencies that call for immediate action. Anyone who lives or works in Marin can register atalertmarin.org, which the county says takes less than five minutes, and list up to five addresses — the county suggests home, work, a child’s school and a family member’s or friend’s house.

Subscribers can also opt into Notification Groups for information that falls short of an emergency alert: significant weather, coastal flooding and king tides, creek and river flooding, prescribed burns and significant traffic disruptions. The groups are not location-based, so a subscriber gets every notice on a topic, wherever in the county it applies.

The county also recommends saving AlertMarin’s number, 877-627-1411, as a phone contact, letting it bypass Do Not Disturb settings and adding a home landline as a second contact method.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Hessel

item.title: Belvedere approves Marin’s first commercial drone delivery rules
item.description: Belvedere City Council voted 3-2 Sept. 14 to advance Marin’s first commercial drone delivery ordinance, barring delivery hubs from homes and limiting where drones can land.
item.content:encoded:
The Belvedere City Council has advanced Marin County’s first ordinance written specifically for commercial drone deliveries, approving it 3-2 after adding protections for public property and privacy.

Councilmembers Jane Cooper and Pat Carapiet voted against the ordinance Sept. 14 after arguing that its proposed delivery hours — beginning at 7 a.m. and extending as late as 11 p.m. — could disturb residents. Mayor Sally Wilkinson, Vice Mayor Kevin Burke and Councilmember Peter Mark supported the measure.

The ordinance is expected to return for a second reading Oct. 12. If adopted, it would take effect 30 days later.

The measure would regulate ground-level activity associated with commercial deliveries, including where drones may land, take off and leave packages. It would not regulate drones while they are in flight because airspace, flight paths, aircraft equipment and pilot requirements fall under the Federal Aviation Administration’s authority.

item.title: Election 2026: Strawberry Rec draws rare race for four-year seats
item.description: Four candidates are running for three four-year seats on the Strawberry Recreation District board Nov. 3, a rare contested race for a district that has struggled to fill seats.
item.content:encoded:
Four candidates are running for three four-year seats on the Strawberry Recreation District board Nov. 3, a rare contested election in a district that has long struggled to find anyone willing to serve.

Chair Peter Teese, a board member since December 2010, is seeking a fifth term. Fellow incumbent Sohrab Saghezchi, a Mill Valley dentist appointed to the board in December 2022 is standing for election to the seat for the first time. The only challenger is David Morgenthaler, a Strawberry father who spent nearly five years in sales and business development at Salesforce.

The fourth candidate, incumbent Sarah Waterfield, declined to comment and did not sit for a portrait.

Election 2026:The Strawberry Recreation District four-year candidates at a glance

Election 2026:Read complete coverage atthearknewspaper.com/election2026

The board voted unanimously Aug. 18 to reject a Marin County civil grand jury recommendation capping special-district members at two consecutive four-year terms, with Teese arguing the district almost never has a contested election and that a limit could empty a seat with no one waiting to fill it. Both of its races are contested this year.

Two other candidates, incumbent Doug Twillman and newcomer Aliza Hawkins, are running for the board’s single two-year seat.

The independent special district serves the unincorporated Strawberry community of about 6,000 residents. Under the board and General Manager Nancy Shapiro, it runs year-round programs, classes, memberships and events and oversees parks, including the dock at Harbor Cove Park. According to the district, property taxes supply only a fraction of its funding from local property taxes — 3.5 cents per dollar of basic tax paid to Marin County, or roughly 15% of its annual revenue. The rest, about $3 million, comes mostly from fees for classes, facility rentals and memberships.

The district hired playground company GameTime in July under a $2.4 million contract to build a playground on grass between the tennis courts and baseball fields at Strawberry Park. A revised quote and a separate bid for a restroom pushed the total past $3 million on Sept. 8, and the board told the company to come back under its $2.5 million ceiling. The playground is expected to open in 2027.

item.title: Salt & Pepper named Tiburon Peninsula business of the year
item.description: Paulino Monterroso started as a dishwasher in a Tiburon cafe in 1992. Now his Salt & Pepper Restaurant on Main Street is the Tiburon chamber’s 2026 Business of the Year.
item.content:encoded:
Salt & Pepper Restaurant, open on Tiburon’s Main Street since 2010, is the Tiburon Peninsula Chamber of Commerce’s 2026 Business of the Year.

It’s the first time the 38 Main St. restaurant has received the honor, says owner Paulino Monterroso, a San Rafael resident.

“It’s an honor to receive this recognition, which is well deserved by all the other businesses, especially as it’s our first year receiving this,” Monterroso says in a Sept. 18 interview at the restaurant, conducted primarily in Spanish. “No. 1, we’re really proud of that.”

The chamber will present the award at its annual awards celebration Nov. 17. Bank of Marin’s annual Spirit of Marin Awards, which recognize the winners of chamber awards across Marin County, also honored Salt & Pepper at the bank’s Sept. 17 luncheon in San Rafael.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez

item.title: Election 2026: Save the date, submit questions for Ark’s Sept. 29 Tiburon council candidates forum
item.description: The Ark is hosting a Tiburon Town Council candidates forum, moderated by the League of Women Voters of Marin County, from 7 to 8:30 p.m. Sept. 29 in the Town Hall council chambers.
item.content:encoded:
The Ark is hosting a Tiburon Town Council candidates forum, moderated by the League of Women Voters of Marin County, from 7 to 8:30 p.m. Sept. 29 in the Town Hall council chambers, 1505 Tiburon Blvd.

Incumbents Alice Fredericks and Jack Ryan face challengers Kathleen Defever, Chuck Hornbrook and Faris Jafar for three seats in the Nov. 3 election.

League volunteers will moderate and keep time for the question-and-answer session. The Community Media Center of Marin will record the forum and post it after the event.

Questions for the candidates can be submitted in advance toforum@thearknewspaper.comor at the event. Candidates will not see the questions ahead of time.

For local election coverage, visitthearknewspaper.com/election2026.

item.title: Tiburon seeks savings as ponds park estimate reaches $3.7 million
item.description: Tiburon parks commissioners asked designers Sept. 15 to trim the cost of a planned park at the former sanitation ponds near McKegney Green, now projected at $3.7 million.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon parks officials are looking for ways to bring down the cost of a park at the former sanitation-ponds site near McKegney Green, where the projected construction price has climbed to $3.7 million.

The Parks, Open Space & Trails Commission asked designers Sept. 15 to reduce the cost of a lawn, price an option for one beach volleyball court instead of two and find savings in a $360,000 shade structure, among other changes to the 60%-complete design. A 60% set fixes a project’s layout and materials and is detailed enough to price, but it is not the final construction drawings.

The meeting followed an informal, hourlong feedback session at which consultants from Mill Valley-based park designers RHAA Landscape Architecture & Planning fielded questions about the park’s design as it stood.

Commissioners also asked the designers to determine whether the proposed adjustable basketball hoops would be strong enough to withstand players hanging on them; to paint the proposed ball wall so it blends into its surroundings; to consider removing some seats closer to McKegney Green; to replace the extended stone seating along the site’s banks with groups of stone seats; and to consider driftwood instead of bike gates on the pedestrian-only curve that connects the Old Rail Trail to the multiuse path in front of the Richardson Bay Sanitary District.

item.title: Tiburon awards $349,000 storm-drain contract as flood fix awaits
item.description: Tiburon Town Council awarded a $349,000 contract Sept. 16 to reline corroded storm drains at nine spots. It won’t fix the flooding at Beach Road and Tiburon Boulevard.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon is paying nearly $350,000 to reline 492 feet of corroded storm drain at nine locations around town — though none of it will stop the water that pools where Beach Road meets Tiburon Boulevard during heavy rain at high tide.

The Town Council awarded the 2026 Storm Drain Rehabilitation Project to Southwest Infrastructure Inc. for $349,024 on Sept. 16, taking the lower of just two bids. It also authorized Town Manager Greg Chanis to approve change orders of up to 10% of the contract, or about $34,902, without returning to the council. The vote was 4-0, with Vice Mayor Isaac Nikfar absent.

The work is trenchless. Crews will clean and repair existing corrugated metal pipe ranging from 10 to 48 inches in diameter, then line it from the inside with cured-in-place pipe, Public Works Engineering Manager David Eshoo told the council. The cured pipe is a new structural sleeve formed within the deteriorated metal, sealing corrosion and extending the pipe’s service life without digging up the street above it.

Storm drains receiving relined pipes, Eshoo said in an email, include a section of Blackfield Drive north of Cecilia Way; two on Karen Way at Leland Way; three along Tiburon Boulevard, at the Belvedere Tennis Club parking lot, at San Rafael Avenue and at Beach Road; and three on southern Paradise Drive, near Mar West Street, Lyford Tower and Mar East Street.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Hessel

item.title: Tiburon parks board scales back Cypress Hollow upgrades
item.description: Tiburon is scaling back its Cypress Hollow Park redesign to the existing play areas and dropping the sidewalk neighbors opposed, cutting a $2.5 million plan at least in half.
item.content:encoded:
Tiburon is scaling back its redesign of Cypress Hollow Park to the existing play structures, dropping the perimeter sidewalk that neighbors objected to and slashing its $2.5 million price tag.

David Eshoo, Tiburon’s Public Works engineering manager and the parks commission’s staff liaison, told the Parks, Open Space & Trails Commission Sept. 15 that the new scope is limited to upgrading the play structures within their current footprints, making an accessible connection between the play areas and improving the grass where needed. Nothing else in the park would be touched. That rules out the larger play areas parents had pressed for; any new equipment has to fit the space that is there.

Santa Rosa-based Carlile Macy, which is designing the upgrades, sent the town a revised plan the day of the meeting.

Eshoo tied the pivot to what the town’s other parks are costing: the Bel Aire play area, projected just north of $1 million, and the former sanitation ponds site near McKegney Green, which designers put at about $3.7 million.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Martinez

item.title: Tiburon Wine Festival returns Oct. 3 with 60 wineries, 10 restaurants
item.description: Honey wine, crab salad and a cover band: The 43rd Tiburon Wine Festival pours from about 60 wineries 1-4 p.m. Oct. 3 at Point Tiburon Plaza.
item.content:encoded:
About 60 wineries and 10 restaurants will pour and serve at Point Tiburon Plaza on Oct. 3, when the Tiburon Peninsula Chamber of Commerce stages the 43rd annual Tiburon Wine Festival.

The event runs 1-4 p.m. and will feature established and small-production wineries from Napa and Sonoma counties and other parts of California.

Tickets cost $139.49, fees included, and all wine tastings and food are included in the price. Proceeds support free chamber events such as the Tiburon Holiday Festival in December and the Friday Nights on Main series, which closes lower Main Street in June and August.

Participating restaurants and food providers include The Bungalow Kitchen, Caffe Acri, The Caprice, Jane/Marin, Luna Blu, Malibu Farm, Salt & Pepper, Trattoria Servino, Tiburon Tavern and Woodlands Market.

item.title: Crib Notes: Belvedere’s ‘Hansel and Gretel House’ draws buyer after two weeks
item.description: Belvedere’s storybook “Hansel and Gretel House” at 246 Beach Road, stripped of its historic designation at the owner’s request, is in contract two weeks after listing at $3.65M.
item.content:encoded:
Belvedere’s “Hansel and Gretel House” is in contract with a buyer about two weeks after the storybook cottage went on the market Aug. 31 at $3.65 million.

The waterfront home at 246 Beach Road drew interest from several prospective buyers before the seller accepted an offer, listing agent Bruce Burman confirmed Sept. 15.

“There were many people interested, and there was one winning offer out of many,” Burman said.

The Belvedere City Council approved the home’s historic designation in August 2023, but owner Gavriel Bar-Or applied in 2026 to have it removed, saying there was no point to the status after the city pulled out of a state program that gives owners of historic homes a property-tax break. Planning and Building Director Rebecca Markwick confirmed Bar-Or completed the required paperwork and that the designation has been removed.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Callister
item.media:description: The storybook-style house at 246 Beach Road in Belvedere, known as the Hansel and Gretel House, is in contract about two weeks after going on the market Aug. 31 at $3.65 million. The City Council designated the 1942 home historic in August 2023, but the city removed that status this year at the owner’s request. (via city of Belvedere 2023)

item.title: Blanch, 18, becomes youngest Tiburon Challenger champion
item.description: Darwin Blanch, 18, of Florida beat No. 4 seed Michael Mmoh 3-6, 6-4, 6-2 Sept. 20 to win the Tiburon Challenger, the youngest champion in the tournament’s history.
item.content:encoded:
Eighteen-year-old Darwin Blanch beat three of the Tiburon Challenger’s top four seeds and came back from a set down to take the men’s singles title, becoming the youngest champion in the tournament’s history.

Blanch, of Boca Raton, Florida, defeated No. 4 seed and 2018 winner Michael Mmoh 3-6, 6-4, 6-2 in the Sept. 20 final at the Tiburon Peninsula Club. It was his first title on the Challenger Tour.

Earlier that afternoon Hans Hach Verdugo of Mexico and American J.J. Tracy beat Nathaniel Lammons and Jackson Withrow in the doubles final in straight sets, 7-6 (7), 6-4.

The finals closed a weeklong tournament with 32 players in the singles main draw and 16 pairs in doubles. In its 18th year the Tiburon Challenger moved up to the ATP Challenger Tour’s 125 level this season, with a $230,000 purse more than double last year’s.

Players in the Challenger Tour are trying to earn enough points to become eligible to enter the ATP Tour and Grand Slam tournaments, which include Wimbledon and the Australian, French and U.S. Opens. The 125 level is named for the number of ranking points its singles champion collects.

Blanch, who turns 19 on Sept. 28, dropped only one set on his way to the final. He came through three sets against compatriot Stefan Kozlov in the round of 32, saving five match points and taking the last of them on a tiebreaker, then took out No. 3 seed Federico Agustin Gomez of Argentina and American qualifier Bryce Nakashima in straight sets in the round of 16 and the quarterfinals.

In the semifinals Sept. 19, Blanch knocked out top seed and reigning champion Michael Zheng in straight sets, 7-6 (5), 7-6 (9), winning both on tiebreakers.

“It was a pretty good week,” Blanch, who entered the tournament ranked No. 245 in the world, said after the match. “Super proud of myself, super proud of my team for the belief, every single day, working. And I’m just super happy for the effort I put in.”

Tennis commentator Mike Cation called Blanch’s forehand “the biggest weapon in the entire draw.”

“And suddenly, the fact he was able to run and get to those forehands a little bit more changed how that match got played,” Cation said after the tournament.

Mmoh, 28, of Bradenton, Florida, came into the week ranked No. 178 in the world. The No. 4 seed beat Karue Sell of Brazil in the round of 32 and American Patrick Maloney in the round of 16. He took his quarterfinal against Abdullah Shelbayh of Jorda...

item.title: Ken Davis
item.description: Ken Davis passed away peacefully on September 9, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Ken Davis passed away peacefully on September 9, 2026, with his loving wife, Ann, by his side. Ken was born and raised in Ohio and attended Ohio Wesleyan University for his BA. He also received his law degree from Duke University and MBA from Stanford Business School. Ken’s entire career was spent with Bank of America and brought him and his young family to Tiburon in the 1960’s. His career took his family to London, England, twice over the years and he retired as Senior Vice President of the bank.

Ken is survived by his wife of 63 years, Ann; his four children, Jeff, Gail, Rick and Bill; as well as nine grandchildren. He enjoyed traveling, hiking, birding, and gardening and was very fond of his many dogs over the years.

item.title: Madeleine ‘Lani’ Stephens Valentine
item.description: Madeleine “Lani” Stephens Valentine died September 9, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
September 28, 1939–September 9, 2026

Madeleine “Lani” Stephens Valentine died the night of September 9, 2026, in Marin County, California, where she had lived for 60 years. She was surrounded by loving family members when she passed.

Lani was born on September 28, 1939, in Mobile, Alabama, the eldest child of Ellen Story Wood and Warren C. Stephens. At a very young age, her family moved west to Hillsborough, CA, where Lani spent her childhood. She graduated from the Convent of the Sacred Heart in Menlo Park in 1956 and graduated from Trinity University in Washington, D.C., in 1960 with a Bachelor of Arts in English literature and a minor in philosophy.

Following college, Lani returned to San Francisco and worked in the Public Relations and Advertising Department of American President Lines. On Valentine’s Day 1966, she married Robert (Bob) Valentine and the two made their home on Corinthian Island in Belvedere, where they raised two children, Tory and Bob, Jr.

Lani grew up at the cusp of the Feminist movement in the 1960’s, and though grounded in the traditional role and values of a stay-at-home mom, through civic and community service she found leadership opportunities and satisfaction.

Lani’s early volunteer work centered on her children’s school and sports activities, serving as president of the Parents Guild and the Tiburon Peninsula Club, and as a docent with the Audubon Canyon Ranch’s Terwilliger Nature Guides program. Over the following decades, her community involvement grew to include the Junior League of San Francisco, where she served as president from 1977 to 1978 and later received the Spirit of the League Award in 1998; the United Way of the Bay Area, as a board member and director; the Marin chapter of Catholic Charities; the American Red Cross; the Marin General Hospital Foundation; the Marin Council of Agencies; and Marin Open Space. In the late 1980s, her focus turned to homelessness in Marin, and she spent three years on the Marin Homeless Commission, one of them as chair, work that helped bring about a year-round shelter at Hamilton.

In 1988, Lani was elected to the Belvedere City Council and served two terms, twice as mayor. She chaired the city’s year-long centennial celebration in 1996 and was named Belvedere’s Citizen of the Year the following year.

Her husband, Bob, passed away in 2015, a few months shy of their 50th wedding anniversary. Together they traveled widely, sharing a lo...

item.title: Travel Bug: Alaska by sea: Bears, glaciers and everything in between
item.description: Tiburon travel writer Marybeth Bond-Sheppard’s fourth trip to Alaska: 13 days from Seattle on Oceania’s Riviera, a small ship that sailed deep into the bay at Hubbard Glacier.
item.content:encoded:
Alaska is America’s last wild frontier — and a land of sublime, overwhelming beauty. The 10 highest major peaks in the U.S. are all in Alaska; many places can be reached only by boat or plane. You can’t even drive to Juneau, the state capital.

We sailed in August, on our fourth trip to Alaska, and we weren’t the only repeat visitors. Many of our fellow passengers on Oceania’s Riviera had been coming back for years, chasing glaciers, whales, bears and bald eagles.

Alaska cruises are booming

The obvious draws are wildlife, glaciers, Indigenous culture and adventure. But talking with other passengers, I found other reasons. Many were from Florida, Georgia, Texas, Arizona and Nevada, escaping a brutal summer heat wave. Others were avoiding the cost and hassle of long-haul international flights in favor of a short hop to the West Coast. As one crew member put it, people are tired of flying overseas. Alaska feels closer to home, and plenty of guests simply love cruising, love Alaska and keep coming back to Oceania for the amenities.

We also appreciated the adults-only atmosphere, which skews toward older, wealthier travelers. We joked that Alaska has become a “last chance” cruise: last chance to see the glaciers before they recede, last chance to make the trip while you still can and last chance to spend a chunk of your portfolio on something unforgettable.
item.dc:creator: Marybeth Bond-Sheppard
item.media:description: Clockwise from top left, a stop at the ‘I Love Prince Rupert’ sign in Prince Rupert, British Columbia, with the ship standing by in the background; morning coffee on deck while cruising the glacier fjords of Holkham Bay in Alaska; a black bear works a salmon run, gorging on eggs before winter; an eagle spreads its wings atop a Tlingit totem pole at Icy Strait Point in Alaska; and a path through the flower beds at Butchart Gardens in Victoria, British Columbia. item.title: Ark audit finds federally linked license-plate searches continue after Tiburon’s Flock safeguards
item.description: A day after The Ark asked Tiburon who approved access to its license-plate cameras, the town revised the policy, dropping the written-request rule and its monthly audit method.
item.content:encoded:
Thirty-four outside police agencies ran 8,542 searches of Tiburon’s license-plate cameras for federally entangled investigations in the seven months after the town rewrote its plate-reader policy in December and began requiring monthly audits, a new Ark audit has found.

More than 4,800 came on or after Feb. 3, when Police Chief Michelle Jean told The Ark the town had worked with vendor Flock Safety “to allow external searches only for valid reasons” — language the town repeated in apublic statement March 9. Every one of the 34 agencies ran at least one of those searches. Twenty-six still have access to the cameras, and eight of those ran searches flagged by The Ark as federally entangled as recently as July.

The Kings County Sheriff’s Office ran 14 on July 2 alone, each naming a Homeland Security Investigations special agent in the search-reason field. Los Angeles County sheriff’s deputies ran nine on July 8 logged as “Assist FBI re: cyber crime” and seven more on July 15 and 16 as “assist fbi taskforce for suspect vehicles in area.”

Tiburon police also allowed a federally funded intelligence center to keep searching the town’s cameras explicitly on behalf of federal agents and out-of-state police for 105 days after The Ark warned the town the searches were barred under California Senate Bill 34, which since 2016 has made it illegal to share plate-reader data with out-of-state, federal and private entities.

Three other organizations did not appear to qualify to receive the data at all, yet they ran 478 searches of Tiburon’s cameras between January and July.

When The Ark asked about those agencies Aug. 6, Police Department officials did not answer, but all three disappeared from Tiburon’s transparency portal on the Flock website within 48 hours. When The Ark inquired about their removal Aug. 10 — seeking records on who had authorized their access and whether required monthly audits had ever identified the agencies — the department again did not answer.

The next day, however, it quietly uploaded a revised license-plate-reader policy to the town website that redefined who qualifies as a share partner, stripped the language requiring written access requests and eliminated the internal audit methodology established Dec. 4.

item.title: Angel Island burn resumes Sept. 23, putting smoke back over the bay
item.description: State Parks, Cal Fire and Marin County Fire plan to resume the Angel Island prescribed burn as early as Sept. 23, putting smoke back over the Tiburon Peninsula.
item.content:encoded:
Crews plan to resume the prescribed burn on Angel Island as early as Sept. 23, putting smoke back over the Tiburon Peninsula and much of the bay two weeks after they called off the same operation partway through.

California State Parks, Cal Fire and the Marin County Fire Department burned just 62 of the 260 acres targeted at Angel Island State Park after igniting Sept. 8, then canceled the rest of that week’s burning after talks with the Bay Area Air Quality Management District. The agencies now say they could keep burning through Sept. 24, depending on wildfire activity, what crews and equipment are free, the weather, how the smoke is predicted to move and how dry the fuel is, according to a joint news release from the Marin County Fire Department and State Parks.

Officials again asked residents not to call 911 to report smoke from the island.

The agencies expect smoke over much of the bay from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. on burn days, and some may still be visible up to three days after ignitions. Officials urged anyone who smells smoke to limit the time they spend in it.

“We work closely with the Air Quality Management District, and we really look for those small windows that have the greatest ability to disperse the smoke in the least impactful manner,” Graham Groneman, a division chief with the Marin County Fire Department, said in the release.

The burn targets fuel loads in the island’s grasslands and coastal scrub and is paid for through Proposition 4, the climate bond voters approved in 2024. State Parks uses prescribed fire there on a rotation and burned vegetation piles on the island in late January.

“We were able to burn 62 acres on the island with the fuels reduction that we’ve accomplished, reducing the chance of a catastrophic fire on the island,” Sean Jerry, a division chief with Cal Fire’s Sonoma Lake Napa Unit, said in the release.

The park stays open on burn days, but portions of the Ida and Sunset trails and the park’s fire and perimeter roads will close during the burn and for one to three days afterward, and the summit of Mount Livermore will be off-limits on some burn days. Officials urged visitors to follow posted closures and directions from park staff and fire crews.

item.title: Election 2026: Four candidates seek three seats on Richardson Bay Sanitary District board
item.description: Incumbents Mark Fitzgerald, Peter McIntosh and Patrick Walravens face challenger John Turnacliff for three Richardson Bay Sanitary District board seats on Nov. 3.
item.content:encoded:
Four Tiburon Peninsula residents are seeking three seats on the Richardson Bay Sanitary District board of directors in the district’s first contested election since 2018.

Incumbents Mark Fitzgerald, Peter McIntosh and Patrick Walravens face challenger John Turnacliff. The three winners will serve four-year terms through November 2030, joining sitting board members Mark Slater and Jeff Slavitz.

Board members receive $125 for every meeting they attend and are eligible for the district’s dental plan.

Election 2026:The Richardson Bay Sanitary District board candidates at a glance

Election 2026:Read complete coverage atthearknewspaper.com/election2026

The Richardson Bay district serves northern Tiburon from Gilmartin Drive to Highway 101 and all of Strawberry from its headquarters at Blackie’s Pasture. It collects wastewater across its service area and pumps it to Mill Valley for treatment through the Sewerage Agency of Southern Marin, a joint-powers agency it belongs to with four other member agencies.

Consolidation was the central question the last time these seats were contested, in 2018, and it is again.

Board members voted unanimously July 21 to reject all seven findings and nine recommendations in a Marin civil grand jury report, “Better Service at Lower Cost — Optimizing Essential Services for the Future of Marin,” that urged the county’s more than 50 special districts, including the Richardson Bay district, to explore consolidation. The report found that fragmented districts duplicate administrative work and leave residents with uneven fees and service levels, thin staffing and weaker long-term resilience.

District officials countered that consolidation had already been studied and that the report failed to account for existing joint operations or the financial risks of merging.

The argument predates this board. A 2011 Marin Local Agency Formation Commission report and a 2018 civil grand jury report both concluded the county had too many sewer agencies, and the Richardson Bay board that year opposed even adding language to its response about exploring consolidation of services on a limited scale. In 2012, at the board’s urging, district ratepayers defeated a ballot proposal to consolidate with other member districts of the Sewerage Agency of Southern Marin.

item.title: Election 2026: The Richardson Bay Sanitary District board candidates at a glance
item.description: The Richardson Bay Sanitary District board candidates at a glance.
item.content:encoded:
Mark Fitzgerald,incumbent

Years as resident:4; grew up in Tiburon.

Occupation:Tiburon Fire Protection District captain.

Education:Fire academy at Butte College; fire-science courses at Santa Rosa Junior College and the College of Marin.

Civic background:Member of the Richardson Bay Sanitary District board since August 2022.

Key issues:Employee continuity, fiscal responsibility, district transparency.

Quote:“I’m proud to be part of that and take the pride and the responsibility of the well-being of the district as kind of a personal affliction. If things go bad there, then I would be part of that. If things go great there, then I was part of that. And the goal is to make everything go well and be good and run smoothly.”

Peter McIntosh,incumbent

Years as resident:15.

Occupation:Co-founder of EnviroSmarts, which makes environmental sensors, including water-leak detectors.

Education:Bachelor’s degree in advertising and communications from Southern Methodist University.

Civic background:Member of the Richardson Bay Sanitary District board since 2021; board president.

Key issues:Continuing good district governance; serving as district liaison to the Sewerage Agency of Southern Marin; bay water quality.

Quote:“Back to the question of what drives me: I just love being a volunteer and helping out. … I’ve done a great job, I think, and I want to continue doing a great job.”

John Turnacliff,challenger

Years as resident:25.

Occupation:Equipment-finance manager; owner of Golden Gate Equipment Finance.

Education:Bachelor’s degree in business administration from the University of Southern California.

Civic background:Chair of the Marin County Republican Central Committee.

Key issues:Improving district operations based on employee feedback; financial stewardship, including limiting rate increases.

Quote:“I’m kind of watching the hen house, the sewer system and what people are doing there for the people that don’t ever want to hear about it or think about it.”

Patrick Walravens,incumbent

Years as resident:26.

Occupation:Managing director and senior equity research analyst at Citizens Capital Markets & Advisory, a Citizens Financial Group subsidiary; began his career as an attorney.

item.title: Election 2026: Measure Z would extend Paradise Cay dredging tax 10 years
item.description: Paradise Cay voters decide Nov. 3 on Measure Z, a parcel tax that pays to dredge the community's canals and its two entry channels to San Francisco Bay.
item.content:encoded:
Voters in Paradise Cay will decide Nov. 3 whether to continue a special parcel tax that pays to dredge the waterfront community’s canals and its two entry channels to San Francisco Bay.

Measure Z would set the tax at $2,200 per lot a year in County Service Area No. 29 beginning July 1, 2027. The rate would then rise automatically by 3% each year beginning July 1, 2028, and the tax would expire June 30, 2037.

The service area estimates the measure would raise an average of about $272,800 a year for maintenance dredging in Paradise Cay’s principal waterways and the north and south entry channels. It needs approval from two-thirds of the votes cast to pass.

Election 2026:Read complete coverage atthearknewspaper.com/election2026

The Marin Board of Supervisors called the election May 19 on a 4-0 vote, with Supervisor Stephanie Moulton-Peters absent. Measure Z would continue an existing special tax scheduled to expire June 30, 2027.

The tax falls on lots inside Service Area No. 29, the county-run district that takes in the Paradise Cay parcels with canal access rather than the whole neighborhood. Keeping those canals and the entrances to the bay navigable requires periodic removal of the sediment that washes into them. Resident Eric Lyons described them as the community’s riparian, or dock-bearing, homeowners. The county has not published how many of the 130 lots pay, though at $2,200 apiece, the revenue estimate works out to about 124.

Lyons has lived in Paradise Cay for more than 30 years and chairs the district’s six-member advisory board. He said the community faces no immediate dredging emergency because its waterways were last dredged in 2020 and 2024. But residents have to keep collecting money for the next project, which the board is planning for 2028 or 2029, he said.

Paradise Cay typically needs dredging about every four or five years, although the precise schedule depends on how quickly sediment accumulates.

“The fill-in depends on many factors, including winter rains, ferry wakes and winter weather in general,” Lyons said. “We’ve never really needed to dredge more frequently than four years, but keeping the north and south cay entry channels clear and wide enough for navigation is always a challenge.”
